Preface

The purpose of this book is to show how algebraic geometry methods can be used to solve different problems in the fields of robotics and control theory, including in the last topic both analysis of dynamic systems and control design.

It is perhaps reductive to see the link between such disciplines based on the fact that algebraic geometry provides algorithms to solve, mostly in an exact manner and often parameterizing sets of solutions, systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities, which are very useful for the design of control laws and observers; as it will be seen throughout the book, algebraic geometry also provides the notions and concepts, such as ideals and varieties, to properly formalize some of the problems under study.

The various applications presented in this book are naturally originated from our previous research experience, and certainly do not exhaust the richness of results that can be obtained in robotics and control theory by using the techniques typical of algebraic geometry; with this in mind, just to help the reader willing to use the same methodologies, we have tried to detail as much as possible our derivations, illustrating with small examples also some of the relatively easy steps, with the purpose of being as much introductory as possible. In some cases, the examples are very simple: this is done on purpose to better emphasize the meaning of the concepts, together with the algorithmic aspects.

It is not assumed that the reader already knows algebraic geometry, only some basic knowledge of calculus and linear algebra is required; therefore, Chapter 1 is devoted to a concise but rigorous exposition of all the basic notions needed in this book; an effort has been made to render the description self contained and to illustrate every concept by examples, most of which simple enough so that computations can be performed by hand. However, such a first chapter is not aimed at a thorough presentation of the topic, so that proofs and also many results that do not find application here are not reported; for a deeper understanding of algebraic geometry the reader is referred to the cited texts, especially Cox et al. (2015).

To further guide the reader to effectively use the proposed methodologies and algorithms, in Chapter it is illustrated how the computations referred to in the examples of Chapter 1 can be performed on Macaulay2, a free CAS (computer algebra system). It is worth stressing that most of the computations described in the book can be performed by other CAS, Macaulay2has been preferred because it is free and complete as for the functionalities needed here.

After the first two chapters, the order of exposition is mostly based on the rationale of postponing further developments of the theory until the chapter or section in which they are used, this means that specifications of the general concepts exposed in Chapter 1 can be found in subsequent sections, just at the point in which they are needed.

As for robotics and control theory, it is assumed that the reader knows the fundamentals of dynamic systems theory and some standard tools in control design, such as Lyapunov stability basic theorems and, as for linear systems, structural properties and observer design principles; however, the problems have been mostly formulated in a self-contained manner, and, only in some cases where to recall more background would have been distracting, references are given to books or papers where the required concepts are introduced. Apart from such references, which are needed to complete or deepen what reported in the book, and others that are at some point necessary to better define our approach, we did not systematically include survey sections in the different chapters; this is due to the number and heterogeneity of the applications considered, it would have been very difficult to obtain a reasonably complete overview on each of the topics touched. We apologize for such an omission and we hope that the references included sufficiently complete this aspect.

About the Authors

Laura Menini received the Laurea degree in 1993 and the Ph.D. in 1997, from the University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy, where she is currently Full Professor. She co-authored the books Symmetries and Semi-invariants in the Analysis of Nonlinear Systems (Springer, 2011) and Mathematical Methods for System Theory (World Scientific, 1998). She is Chair of the IFAC Coordinating Committee 2 — Design Method and Senior Editor of the IEEE Control Systems Letters.

Corrado Possieri received his Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Medical Engineering and his Ph.D. degree in Computer Science, Control and Geoinformation from the University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy, in 2011, 2013, and 2016, respectively. In 2016, he visited the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). In 2018, he joined the Department of Electronics and Telecommunications at Politecnico di Torino, where he was an Assistant Professor. Subsequently, in 2019, he joined the Institute for Systems Analysis and Computer Science of the National Research Council of Italy (IASI-CNR), where he is currently a Researcher. He is Associate Editor of IEEE CSS Conference Editorial Board, of the EUCA Conference Editorial Board, and of the IFAC Conference Editorial Board.

Antonio Tornambè is currently Full Professor of Control Theory at University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy. His research interests include control theory for linear and nonlinear systems. He is the co-author of Discrete-Event System Theory: An Introduction (World Scientific, 1995), Mathematical Methods for System Theory (World Scientific, 1998), and Symmetries and Semi-invariants in the Analysis of Nonlinear Systems (Springer, 2011).

Chapter 1

Algebraic Geometry Notions

1.1 Affine varieties and polynomial ideals

A monomial in the single variables x1, . . . , xn is a product of the form

where the αi’s are non-negative integers. Let x denote x = [x1 . . . xn]⊤. To shorten the notation, the product in (1.1) is also written as xα, where α = (α1, . . . , αn) is the ordered tuple (referred to as multi–index) of the exponents in the monomial. The total degree of xα, denoted |α|, is defined as the sum of the exponents, i.e., |α| := α1 + · · · + αn. In the following, any tuple is considered ordered.

Let be a field, such as, e.g., , or , i.e., the set of rational, real or complex numbers, respectively. Whenever a problem is to be recast in an algebraic geometry setting, it is needed to specify at the very beginning which is the field used for the analysis. Such a field is referred to as ambient field. When a change of ambient field is necessary for some of the steps of the problem solution, this is specified and, if convenient, emphasized with appropriate notation. Let be the set of integers. Given m ∈ , the symbol m denotes the set of integers greater than or equal to m. Similarly, given r ∈ , the symbol r denotes the set of real numbers greater than or equal to r.

A polynomial p in x, with coefficients in the field , is a finite -linear combination of monomials and is written as follows:

where is a finite set (without repetitions) of tuples α = (α1, . . . , αn), with αi ∈ 0, i = 1, . . . , n; if all coefficients aα, α ∈ , are zero, the corresponding polynomial is referred to as the zero polynomial. A product of a non-zero element in and a monomial appearing in a polynomial (i.e., one of the aαxα’s appearing in (1.2), with aα ≠ 0) is referred to as a term of the polynomial. The total degree deg(p) of a polynomial p is the maximum of the total degrees of the monomials appearing in its terms (it is pointed out that all terms aαxα in p have a non-zero coefficient aα). The total degree of the zero polynomial is not defined, because the set of the terms of the zero polynomial is empty. For a polynomial p in a single variable, the total degree coincides with the usual degree of p.

Let [x1, . . . , xn] (or, briefly, [x]) be the ring of all polynomials in x1, . . . , xn with coefficients in the ambient field ; when working with polynomials in [x], the ring [x] is called the ambient ring. Note that it is preferable to specify which is the ambient ring, because, whereas it seems natural to consider the polynomial

in the ambient ring [x1, x2, x3], for the polynomial

it is not so obvious if it has to be considered in the ambient ring [x1, x2, x3] or in ()[x1, x2, x3], where () is the smallest finite algebraic extension of containing .

A rational function in x with coefficients in the field is a quotient , where p and q are polynomials in [x] and q is different from the zero polynomial. Two rational functions and are equal if paqb−pbqa is the zero polynomial in [x]. It is worth pointing out that the set of the rational functions in x with coefficients in has the mathematical structure of a field and is denoted, in the following, through the symbols (x) and frac([x]).

Given a field and a positive integer n, define the n-dimensional affine space over as

Polynomials can easily be related to affine spaces. The key idea is that any polynomial p ∈ [x] yields a polynomial function (denoted with the same symbol)

which associates to any x̂ ∈ n a unique p(x̂), which is obtained through the substitution x = x̂ in the polynomial p. Note that if is not finite as a field (as, for instance, , or ), then p is the zero polynomial in [x] if and only if the corresponding polynomial function p : n → is zero, p(x̂) = 0, for all x̂ ∈ . On the other hand, if is a finite field (i.e., a field constituted by a finite number of elements), there may be non-zero polynomials p in [x] such that the corresponding polynomial function p : n → satisfies p(x̂) = 0, ∀x̂ ∈ , as shown in the following example.

Different ambient rings constitute different mathematical entities. Hence, given p1(x) = x in [x] and p2(x, y) = 3x + y in [x, y], where x and y are single variables, it makes no sense to define the sum p1 + p2. However, each polynomial in [x] can also be thought of as a polynomial in [x, y] and, therefore, with the coercion of p1 in [x, y], the sum p1 +p2 makes sense. Thus, coercion is a fundamental tool that can be used when working with polynomials belonging to different rings.

The coercion can operate at different levels; in particular, if 1 and 2 are two fields such that 1 ⊆ 2, any element in 1[x1, . . . , xn] can be coerced into 2[x1, . . . , xn], or, considering the additional single variables y1, . . . , ym, any element in 1[x1, . . . , xn] can be coerced into either 1[x1, . . . , xn, y1, . . . , ym] or 2[x1, . . . , xn, y1, . . . , ym].

The field is said to be algebraically closed if any non-constant polynomial in [z], where z is a single variable, has a root in . For instance, is not algebraically closed because the roots of z2 + 1 are not in , whereas is algebraically closed because, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Cox et al., 2015, Theorem 7 at page 4), any polynomial in [z] has a root in .

1.2 Monomial orders and Gröbner bases

In Section 1.1, the basic notions of commutative algebra on polynomial rings and of geometry of affine varieties have been introduced and the connections between them have been highlighted. In this section, the basic notions of computational algebraic geometry, which allow one to solve problems about ideals in an algorithmic fashion, are recalled.

There are three kinds of elementary operations that can be carried out on the rows of a matrix M ∈ m×n:

(i) Interchange two rows.

(ii) Multiply a row by a non-zero scalar in .

(iii) Add to a row any other row multiplied by a scalar in .

A row echelon form (M) of a matrix M ∈ m×n, which can always be obtained by a finite sequence of elementary operations on the rows of M, satisfies:

(a) All non-zero rows of (M) precede all its zero rows.

(b) The first non-zero entry in a non-zero row of (M) (which is called the leading coefficient of the row, or pivot) appears to the right of the first non-zero entry in the preceding row.

(c) The leading coefficients of (M) are all equal to 1.

If, in addition to the above properties (a)–(c), one has that

(d) the leading coefficient is the only non-zero entry in its column,

such a row echelon form of M is said to be reduced and is denoted r(M); r(M) can always be obtained by a finite sequence of elementary operations on the rows of M. Unlike a row echelon form, the reduced row echelon form is uniquely determined, because it does not depend on the sequence of elementary operations used for its computation.

A row echelon form and the reduced row echelon form of a matrix M can be computed through the Gauss and Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithms (Meyer, 2000), respectively. The Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm is reported in the following, where the symbol [M]k,j is used to denote the (k, j)th entry of M.

The main goal of the remainder of this section and of the following sections is to extend the univariate polynomial division algorithm and the elimination features of the Gauss–Jordan algorithm to the case of multivariate polynomials. Analyzing the univariate polynomial division and the Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithms, one can observe that the notion of order is a key topic of both these algorithms. In fact, to perform the division algorithm between two univariate polynomials, one is implicitly using the degree order on the single variable monomials,

where z is a single variable, whereas, to perform the Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm, one is implicitly using the following order of the single variables:

Clearly, to consider multivariate polynomials, one has to combine both the above orders somehow.

A possible approach to extend the above orders to multivariate polynomials is to introduce the notion of monomial order, i.e., an order on the terms of the polynomials belonging to [x1, . . . , xn]. First, note that each monomial is uniquely determined by the tuple of exponents α = (α1, . . . , αn), and vice versa. Therefore, any order ≻ established on the tuples α gives an order on the monomials xα. With this equivalence in mind, a monomial order on [x], denoted ≻, is a relation on the set of monomials xα such that:

(i) ≻ is a total order, i.e., for each pair xα, xγ, either xα ≻ xγ, or xα = xγ or xα ≺ xγ;

(ii) given xα, xγ such that xα ≻ xγ and a multi-index δ, one has that xα+δ ≻ xγ+δ;

(iii) ≻ is a well order, i.e., each non-empty set of monomials has a smallest element.

Two important examples of monomial orders are the lexicographic order (briefly, Lex monomial order), denoted ≻Lex, and the graded reverse lexicographic order (briefly, GRL monomial order), denoted ≻GRL. Let α, γ ∈ be given. One has that α ≻Lex γ (or, equivalently, xα ≻Lex xγ, with x1 ≻Lex . . . ≻Lex xn), if the first nonzero entry of the vector difference α − γ is positive. On the other hand, one has that α ≻GRL γ (or, equivalently, xα ≻GRL xγ, with x1 ≻GRL . . . ≻GRL xn), if |α| > |γ|, or |α| = |γ| and the last non-zero entry of α − γ is negative. Clearly, these two orders may arrange the monomials in [x] in different ways.

To overcome this non-uniqueness issue, a possible approach is to divide by an ideal instead of a given tuple of polynomials, which means using a “special” set of generators of with the property that the remainder r of the division of any polynomial by this set of generators is uniquely determined and that the condition r = 0 is equivalent to membership in . In the following, it is shown that the Gröbner bases have these two nice properties.

Using the convention 〈〉 = {0}, the empty set is thought of as the Gröbner basis of the zero ideal {0}. With this convention, it turns out that any ideal in [x] admits a (not necessarily unique) Gröbner basis and any Gröbner basis of an ideal is actually a basis of (Buchberger, 2006). A Gröbner basis = {g1, . . . , gm} is said to be reduced if LC(gi) = 1, i = 1, . . . , m, and gi is reduced with respect to (g1, . . . , gi−1, gi+1, . . . , gm) (i.e., no monomial of gi lies in 〈LT( \ {gi})〉). Any ideal has a unique reduced Gröbner basis with respect to the chosen monomial order.

Note that the coefficients of the polynomials in a Gröbner basis of an ideal in [x] are ratios of, often big, elements of (similarly, when = (β), for some vector β of parameters); if convenient, to simplify the expressions of such polynomials, all denominators are cleared, without explicit mention, from which the condition LC(gi) = 1, i = 1, . . . , m, need not hold in the reported examples of reduced Gröbner bases.

An interesting property of Gröbner bases is that, once any monomial order has been chosen on [x], although a Gröbner basis of an ideal in [x] is not unique, for any polynomial p ∈ [x], the remainder of the division of p by is unique; to point out the independence from of the remainder of the division of p by , such a remainder is denoted p% and called the normal form of p by . In addition, if p% = 0 for some monomial order, then it is zero for any other monomial order. Hence, the use of Gröbner bases completely solves the ideal membership problem, because p ∈ if and only if p% = 0 for some monomial order.

An algorithm to compute a Gröbner basis of a given ideal is given in Cox et al. (2015, Theorem 2 at page 91) and is summarized in Algorithm 1.2.4.

Algorithm 1.2.4: The Buchberger algorithm.

Remark 1.2.1. Some comments about such an algorithm are given to allow the reader to better understand Algorithm 1.2.4. The polynomial s defined at Step 7 is called the S-polynomial of p and q, denoted S(p, q). It is worth mentioning that such a polynomial is in the ideal 〈p, q〉 and that it is specifically designed to produce the cancellation of the leading terms of p and q. In Buchberger (2006), it has been proved that = {g1, . . . , gr} is a Gröbner basis of the ideal if and only if, for all pairs i ≠ j, the remainder of the division of S(gi, gj) by the elements of (listed in arbitrary order) is zero (this fact is usually known as the Buchberger criterion). Hence, the algorithm terminates at Step 13 providing a Gröbner basis of the ideal = 〈p1, . . . , ps〉. However, such a basis is not in general reduced, because the generators p1, . . . , ps of the ideal are always contained in a basis thus obtained. In fact, the algorithm extends the basis {p1, . . . , ps} by successively appending non-zero remainders of the division of S(gi, gj) by (g1, . . . , gr). This iterative extension of the ideal basis suggests the complexity underlying the computation of Gröbner bases. In fact, it has been proved (Bardet, 2005) that the computation of Gröbner bases is an EXPSPACE-complete problem. However, as shown in Lazard (1983), the running time and storage space required for the computation of a Gröbner basis seem to be manageable “on average” by a modern computer, making it possible to efficiently apply such tools.

1.3 Homogeneous polynomials and ideals

A polynomial p ∈ [x] is homogeneous of total degree d (it is referred to as a form of total degree d) if each monomial in p has total degree d. Given p ∈ [x], let pd be the sum of all terms of p of total degree d; each pd is homogeneous, p = ∑d pd, and the pd’s are called the homogeneous components of p.

Definition 1.3.1. An ideal in [x] is homogeneous if for any p ∈ , the homogeneous components of p are in as well.

1.4 Elimination theory

In this section, the basic notions of the elimination theory are briefly recalled, describing the process of elimination of variables from a system of polynomial equations. Such a process extends the Gauss–Jordan algorithm to nonlinear systems of polynomial equations and is of great help in the subsequent development of control theory applications.

The polynomials p1, . . . , ps ∈ [x] are linearly dependent if there are m scalars c1, . . . , cm ∈ , not all zero, such that c1p1 +. . . +cmps is the zero polynomial in [x] (linearly independent, otherwise). The polynomials p1, . . . , ps ∈ [x] are algebraically dependent if there is a non-zero polynomial q ∈ [y1, . . . , ym] such that q(p1(x), . . . , ps(x)) is the zero polynomial in [x] (algebraically independent, otherwise). Clearly, linear dependence implies algebraic dependence (if c1p1 + · · · + cmps = 0, then one can take q(y1, . . . , ys) = c1y1 + · · · + csys), whereas algebraic independence implies linear independence.

Congruence modulo is an equivalence relation on [x], namely, the following properties hold:

(i) p = p mod .

(ii) If p = q mod , then q = p mod .

(iii) If p = q mod and q = r mod , then p = r mod .

Theorem 1.6.1 (Finiteness Theorem, Cox et al., 2006, Theorem 6 at page 251). Let be an ideal in [x], and be a Gröbner basis of , with respect to any monomial order. Consider the following conditions:

(1.6.1.5) The affine variety V() is a finite set.

Then, conditions (1.6.1.1)–(1.6.1.4) are equivalent and they all imply (1.6.1.5). If, in addition, the field is algebraically closed, then (1.6.1.1)–(1.6.1.5)are equivalent.

If is an ideal in [x] such that one of the conditions (1.6.1.1)–(1.6.1.4) of Theorem 1.6.1 hold, then is called zero-dimensional, reflecting the fact that V() is constituted just by a finite number of points. In particular, the number of points in V() is never greater than the number of monomials in ; if is algebraically closed and is radical, then the number of points in V() is equal to the number of monomials in .

1.7 Root localization

Before tackling the problem of root localization, some notions are recalled about symmetric matrices and quadratic forms.

Let Q be a symmetric square matrix in m×m, and let q(ξ) = ξ⊤Qξ be the associated quadratic form, where ξ = [ξ1 . . . ξm]⊤. Any non-singular matrix V ∈ m×m transforms Q into another symmetric matrix Q̌ = V⊤QV in m×m; matrices Q and Q̌ are referred to as congruent, with ξ = V being the corresponding congruence transformation. One has ξ⊤Qξ = ⊤V⊤QV = ⊤Q̌, from which q̌() = ⊤Q̌ is the quadratic form associated with Q̌.

Lemma 1.7.1. For any Q ∈ m×m, there is V ∈ m×m, det(V) ≠ 0, such that Q̌ = V⊤QV ∈ m×m is diagonal, with the entries on the main diagonal in the set {−1, 0, +1}. Equivalently, any quadratic form q(ξ) = ξ⊤Qξ can be diagonalized by a congruence transformation ξ = V , V ∈ m×m, det(V) ≠ 0, thus obtaining a weighted sum of squares q̌() = with the weights ci ∈ {−1, 0, +1}, i = 1, . . . , n.

Proof. Any symmetric Q ∈ m×m has real eigenvalues and can be diagonalized by a linear transformation, i.e., it admits a decomposition of the form Q = W ΛW −1, where the columns of W are eigenvectors of Q and Λ is diagonal, with the eigenvalues of Q on the main diagonal, Λ = diag(λ1, . . . , λm). Actually, matrix W can always be chosen so that W −1 = W⊤, which implies Q = W ΛW⊤. Letting

and Γ = diag(γ1, . . . , γm), the lemma is proved by taking V = W · Γ−1.

The number of −1’s on the main diagonal of Q̌, denoted #−(Q), is called the negative index of inertia of Q, the number of 0’s on the main diagonal of Q̌, denoted #0(Q), is called the nullity index of inertia of Q, and the number of +1’s on the main diagonal of Q̌, denoted #+(Q), is called the positive index of inertia of Q; this three numbers satisfy

The triple (#−(Q), #0(Q), #+(Q)) is called the inertia triple of Q, and is denoted i(Q). The signature of Q is (Q) := #+(Q) − #−(Q). By (1.27), the inertia triple i(Q) and the couple (#0(Q), (Q)) give the same information about Q. The dimension of the nullspace of Q is #0(Q), and #−(Q)+#+(Q) is the rank of Q. If i(Q) = (m−, m0, m+), with m−, m0, m+ ∈ 0, m = m− + m0 + m+, is the inertia triple of matrix Q, matrix Q̌ in Lemma 1.7.1 can always be taken as

by possibly reordering the columns of V .

The following corollary follows from the above discussion.

Corollary 1.7.1. The triple (m−, m0, m+), with m−, m0, m+ ∈ 0, m = m− + m0 + m+, is the inertia triple of a symmetric matrix Q ∈ m×m if and only if there exist m− +m+ linear forms ωi ∈ [ξ], being linearly independent, such that

The following lemma states the Sylvester law of inertia, namely that the inertia triple of a symmetric matrix in m×m is invariant with respect to congruence transformations.

Lemma 1.7.2 (The Sylvester Law of Inertia, Carrell, 2017, Theorem 9.13). For any symmetric Q ∈ m×m, one has

In particular, for Q, Q̌ ∈ m×m, if i(Q) = i(Q̌), then there exists V ∈ m×m, det(V) ≠ 0, such that Q̌ = V⊤QV .

There are mainly two possibilities for computing the inertia triple of a symmetric matrix Q: one is based on the (numerical, in most of the cases) computation of the eigenvalues of Q, and the other is based on the application of the classical Descartes Rule of Signs to the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of Q (which does not require any numerical approximation if the entries of Q are rational numbers). If Q has entries in , then the application of the Descartes Rule of Signs gives certificated values for the inertia triple and signature, i.e., obtained without any numerical approximation.

An infinite-dimensional matrix (such as Hσ) is said to have finite rank r if all the determinants of its minors of dimension greater than r are zero but there is at least one non-zero determinant of a minor of dimension r. Kronecker has proved that the infinite matrix Hσ has finite rank if and only if and only if the formal series is convergent for all ẑ in a neighborhood of z = 0, and its sum σ(ẑ), for ẑ ∈ , is a rational function of ẑ; in this case, the number of poles of the rational function σ(z) is r − 1, where r is the rank of matrix Hσ; in particular, the leading principal minor of Hσ of dimension r has determinant different from zero.

The mth leading principal minor of a square matrix M is the matrix obtained by deleting all but the first m rows and columns of M.

(1.7.5.2) #0(T〈p〉,h) = #p,0 + #p,0.

(1.7.5.3) #+(T〈p〉,h) = #p,+ + p,≠0/2.

(1.7.5.4) (T〈p〉,h) = #p,+ − #p,−.

Proof. Let q〈p〉,h(ξ) be the quadratic form associated with T〈p〉,h,

Since p is square free, the roots ẑ1, . . . , ẑm are distinct, from which the associated Vandermonde matrix V (ẑ1, . . . , ẑm) is invertible, and, therefore, the m linear forms ξ1 + ẑiξ2 + · · · + ξm are linearly independent. One has the following cases:

(i) If h(ẑi) = 0, then h(ẑi)·(ξ1+ẑiξ2+· · ·+ξm)2 = 0, regardless of whether ẑi is real or non-real.

(ii) If ẑi is real and h(ẑi) > 0, then h(ẑi)·(ξ1+ẑiξ2+· · ·+ξm)2 = · (ξ1 + ẑiξ2 + · · · + ξm))2 is a square of a real linear form, with coefficient +1.

(iii) If ẑi is real and h(ẑi) < 0, then h(ẑi)·(ξ1+ẑiξ2+· · ·+ξm)2 = −((ξ1+ẑiξ2+· · ·+ξm))2 is a square of a real linear form, with coefficient −1.

(iv) If ẑi is non-real and h(ẑi) ≠ 0, then the sum of h(ẑi)·(ξ1 +ẑiξ2 + · · · + ξm)2 and of its complex conjugate yields two squares of real linear forms, one with coefficient +1 and the other one with coefficient −1.

Then, (1.7.5.2) follows from (i), (1.7.5.1) follows from (iii) and (iv), and (1.7.5.3) follows from (ii) and (iv). Finally, (1.7.5.4) follows from (1.7.5.1) and (1.7.5.3).

The following Shape Lemma establishes the elimination properties of the Lex monomial order.

Lemma 1.8.1 (Shape Lemma, Sturmfels, 2002, Proposition 2.3). Let be an ideal in [x], being radical and zero-dimensional, and let d be the number of points in V(). Apart from a reordering of the variables, assume that the d points belonging to V() have distinct xn-coordinates, and fix the Lex monomial order, with x1 ≻Lex . . . ≻Lex xn. The reduced Gröbner basis of is

where

with q1, . . . , qn ∈ [xn], deg(qn) = d and deg(qi) d − 1, i = 1, . . . , n − 1.

Hence, one can compute the coordinates of all points in V() computing the d roots of the univariate polynomial qn(xn) in xn, and substituting such values into x1 = q1(xn), . . . , xn−1 = qn−1(xn).

If the d points belonging to V() have distinct xn-coordinates, then one can say that xn is separating for V().

The reduced Gröbner basis of an ideal (with respect to the Lex monomial order, with x1 ≻Lex . . . ≻Lex xn) need not be in the Shape Lemma form when one or more of the following cases arise:

(i) is not radical.

(ii) For any reordering of the variables, xn is never separating for V().

(iii) is not zero-dimensional.

If the purpose is to find the points in V(), then the above cases can be dealt with as follows:

(i) Since V() = V( ), replace with .

(ii) There are two possibilities:

• Take “at random” a linear change of variables y = Ax, until the resulting yn is separating for the ideal expressed in the y-coordinates.

• Introduce an auxiliary single variable xn+1 and take “at random” a linear polynomial q in [x1, . . . , xn], until xn+1 is separating for the ideal + 〈xn+1 − q(x1, . . . , xn)〉 in the larger ambient ring [x1, . . . , xn, xn+1].

(iii) Consider some of the variables, say x1, . . . , xℓ, as parameters and let (x1, . . . , xℓ)[xℓ+1, . . . , xn] be the ambient ring.

1.10 Modules and syzygies

If [x1, . . . , xn] is the ring of the polynomials in x, with coefficients in the field , then the set m[x1, . . . , xn], m ∈ 1, of the vectors, whose m entries are polynomials in the ring [x1, . . . , xn], is a module over the ring [x]; in the following, the elements of the ambient module m[x] are referred to as polynomial vectors. A module over a ring is a generalization of the notion of vector space over a field, where the scalars are the elements of the ring, the addition is defined between elements of the module, and the multiplication is defined between elements of the ring and elements of the module: given two polynomial vectors p, q ∈ m[x], with entries pi, qi ∈ [x], and one polynomial scalar c ∈ [x], one has p + q ∈ m[x] and cp ∈ m[x], with [p+q]i = pi +qi, and [cp]i = cpi, i = 1, . . . , m, where [·]i denotes the ith entry of the vector at argument.

If p1, . . . , ps are generators of some sub-module in m[x], = 〈p1, . . . , ps〉, then {p1, . . . , ps} is said to be a basis of , and P = [p1 . . . ps] ∈ m×s[x] is referred to as a presentation matrix of . For P = [p1 . . . ps] ∈ m×s[x], 〈P〉 is used to denote the sub-module generated by the columns of P (i.e., 〈P〉 = 〈p1, . . . , ps〉).

The nice properties of a Gröbner basis of an ideal with respect to division immediately extend to this new setting. Namely, if = {g1, . . . , gk} is a Gröbner basis of a sub–module ⊆ m[x], then p ∈ if and only if the remainder of the division of p by the tuple (g1, . . . , gk) is zero. As for Gröbner bases of ideals in [x], a Gröbner basis of a sub-module in m[x] is reduced if LC(gi) = 1, i = 1, . . . , k, and gi is reduced with respect to {g1, . . . , gi−1, gi+1, . . . , gk} (i.e., LT(gi) is not divisible by any one of the leading terms LT(g1), . . . , LT(gi−1), LT(gi+1), . . . , LT(gk)). Furthermore, any sub-module ⊆ m[x] admits a unique reduced Gröbner basis.

Sub-modules of m[x] can exhibit behaviors very different from vector spaces. For instance, it is well known from linear algebra that a basis of a vector space is constituted by vectors that are linearly independent and any vector in the vector space is a -linear combination of these vectors. This need not be true for sub-modules of m[x], since the scalars are taken in [x]. Consider, for instance, the polynomial vectors p1, p2, p3 of Example 1.10.1. It can easily be checked that {p1, p2, p3} is a reduced Gröbner basis for = 〈p1, p2, p3〉 and that c1(x) = −x3, c2(x) = x2, c3(x) = x1 are such that c1p1 + c2p2 + c3p3 is the zero polynomial vector. This example shows that, unlike vector spaces, sub-modules need not have bases that are [x]-linearly independent. More generally, no sub-module in 1[x], which is not principal and non-zero, can be generated by a [x]-linearly independent set. In fact, any pair of polynomials p1, p2 ∈ [x] satisfy a non-trivial [x]-linear dependence, because p2p1 − p1p2 = 0.

Chapter 2

Implementations in Macaulay2

2.1 The Macaulay2 language

Most of the computations reported in this book have been carried out using Macaulay2 (Grayson and Stillman, 2020), a free, open-source computer algebra system for computations in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. The objective of this chapter is to provide some snippets of code, to introduce the reader to the use of Macaulay2. This is far from being a complete and general introduction to this system, but it is rather an applicative commentary to the theory resumed in Chapter 1.

To do polynomial computations with Macaulay2, one must fix the ambient ring to which the polynomials belong and fix a monomial order on it. For instance, to fix the ambient ring [x1, . . . , x4] and the Lex monomial order, with x1 ≻Lex . . . ≻Lex x4, one can use the following input instruction:

i1 : R = QQ[x_1..x_4, MonomialOrder => Lex]

where i1 represents the input prompt; executing this instruction generates two lines of output labeled o1 showing the name of the output

o1 = R

and the type of the output:

o1 : PolynomialRing

The QQ is the Macaulay2 instruction for the field (the fields and of the real and complex numbers, respectively, are represented by RR and CC), whereas Lex stands for the Lex monomial order (the GRL monomial order is fixed by GRevLex, whereas the elimination order that eliminates the first i variables from the start of the list is fixed by MonomialOrder => Elimination i). The order on the ring variables is specified by the list in the square brackets.

Once any monomial order on the ambient ring has been chosen, the polynomials p1(x) = x1 − + x3 and p2(x) = + x2 + x4 are assigned to p1 and p2, respectively, with the instructions:

p1 = x_1-x_2^2+x_3

p2 = x_1^4+x_2*x_3^2+x_4

Then, the ideal 〈p1, p2〉 is assigned to I with the instruction:

I = ideal(p1,p2)

whereas

G = gens gb I

computes the reduced Gröbner basis of I and assign to G the result as a one-row matrix of polynomials.

The remainder of the division of the polynomial +++−1 by is computed by

(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2-1) % I

Macaulay2 allows very general coefficient fields in polynomial rings. For instance, to fix the polynomial ring (u1, u2)[x1, x2] (i.e., the ring of polynomials in x1, x2, with coefficients in the field of the rational functions (u1, u2)) and the GRL monomial order, with x2 ≻GRL x1, the following instruction can be used:

R = frac(QQ[u_1,u_2])[x_2,x_1, MonomialOrder => GRevLex]

Quotient rings can be fixed in Macaulay2 as well. For instance, the ring [x1]/〈 + 1〉 is fixed as

QR = QQ[x_1]/ideal(x_1^2+1)

The leading term, leading monomial, and leading coefficient of a polynomial (with respect to the chosen monomial order) are computed by leadTerm, leadMonomial, and leadCoefficient, respectively. The leadTerm instruction can also be applied to an ideal and the output is a set of generators for 〈LT()〉.

Macaulay2 can carry out also operations on ideals. Hence, if the ideals and are represented by I and J, one can compute

• the sum of and as I+J,

• the product of and as I*J,

• the intersection of and as intersect(I,J),

• the quotient of by as I:J,

• the saturation of by as saturate(I,J).

The radical of the ideal represented by I is computed and its generators are presented by

gens radical(I)

The above instruction returns a set of generators of the radical of the ideal represented by I as a row vector.

Macaulay2 is also able to carry out operations on modules and sub-modules. Before working with a sub-module in m[x], the base ring has to be fixed as in the case of polynomial ideals. To fix the Lex monomial order, with the TOP⇓ extension, as it has been introduced in Section 1.10, one can use the instruction MonomialOrder => {Lex, Position => Down}, whereas the POT⇓ extension of the GRL monomial order can be fixed with the instruction MonomialOrder => {Position => Down, GRevLex}. As for polynomial ideals, the order on the ring variables is specified by the list in the square brackets.

The presentation matrix of a sub-module can be obtained through the instruction matrix. For instance, the matrix

can be set through the instruction

P = matrix{{x_1^2+x_2,x_1-x_3,x_4},{x_2^2+x_1, 0,-x_3}}

Then, the sub-module whose presentation matrix is P can be generated as

M = image P

The reduced Gröbner basis of the module M with respect to the chosen monomial order can be computed using the instruction

gens gb M

which returns the reduced Gröbner basis of M through the corresponding presentation matrix. Finally, a syzygy matrix of P can be computed as

syz P

Chapter 3

The Inverse Kinematics of Robot Arms

3.1 The direct kinematics

A robot arm can be represented by a set of n+1 rigid links connected by n joints (either of rotational or linear type, with one degree of freedom). The links are the rigid members connecting the joints, and the joints are the movable parts of the robot that cause relative motion between adjacent links. If the joints are of linear type, then the relative motion between adjacent links is a translation, whereas, if the joints are of rotational type, then the relative motion is a rotation. Let the links of the robot be numbered from 0 to n (the 0th link is the base of the robot, whereas the nth link corresponds to the endeffector). The joints are numbered from 1 to n: the ith joint connects the (i − 1)th link with the ith one, i = 1, 2, . . . , n. The generalized coordinate representing the displacement of the ith joint is qi: qi is a distance if the ith joint is of linear type, whereas qi is an angle if the ith joint is of rotational type. Define n+1 reference frames, each one attached to one link: the reference frame i is attached to the ith link, i = 0, 1, . . . , n, so that 0 is an inertial frame, and the origin of n is located on the end-effector.

Example 3.1.1. Consider the robot arm depicted in Figure 3.1 with three rotational links. In such a figure, the symbol ◦ (respectively, ×) denotes a vector orthogonal to the plane of representation that exits from (respectively, enters in) such a plane. This notation is used for all robotic structures reported hereafter. Note that the links are numbered from 0 (base of the robot) to 3 (end-effector) and that the joints are numbered from 1 to 3. Namely, the joint whose generalized coordinate is q1 (respectively, q2, q3) connects the 0th and 1st (respectively, the 1st and the 2nd, the 2nd and the 3rd) links. The reference frame 0(x0, y0, z0) is attached to the 0th link and, hence, it is an inertial frame. On the other hand, the reference frame 3(x3, y3, z3) is attached to the end-effector.

One of the most commonly used methods to place the reference frames 0, . . . , n is the Denavit–Hartenberg procedure, which is summarized in Algorithm 3.1.1.

Algorithm 3.1.1: Denavit–Hartenberg procedure.

If the Denavit–Hartenberg procedure outlined in Algorithm 3.1.1 is used in the collocation of the reference frames, each transformation matrix Qi−1,i is the product of four elementary transformation matrices, depending on four parameters (θi, di, αi, ai):

this corresponds to a rotation about the z-axis of an angle θi, followed by a translation along the z-axis of a displacement di, followed by a rotation about the x-axis of an angle αi, followed by a translation along the x-axis of a displacement a. This means that the relative motion of two adjacent links is described by the following parameters:

(i) θi is the joint angle,

(ii) di is the link offset,

(iii) αi is the link twist,

(iv) ai is the link length.

When dealing with robot arms, these parameters can be summarized in a table, referred to as the Denavit–Hartenberg table, that summarizes the sequence of elementary operations (i.e., rotations and translations) required to move the reference frame 0 into the reference frame n.

Most robot arms can be divided into two parts: the first part is the arm-and-body section, with three degrees of freedom; the second part is usually a spherical wrist, with three degrees of freedom. The aim of the arm-and-body section is to locate the end-effector of the robot at some point of the workspace, whereas the aim of the spherical wrist is to give the orientation to the robot end-effector. In fact, when dealing with most robot arms, the position and orientation direct kinematics can be decoupled through the following steps:

(1) given the desired position and orientation of the end effector, determine the target position of the arm-and-body section;

(2) solve the position inverse kinematics problem for the arm-andbody section;

(3) considering the orientation resulting from the solution to the position inverse kinematics and the target orientation, solve the orientation inverse kinematics problem for the spherical wrist.

Therefore, in most cases, the position and orientation direct kinematics can be considered disjointedly, as in this chapter.

The problem of determining the inverse orientation is instead considered in Section 3.4.

3.2 The inverse kinematics

Solving the inverse kinematics problem consists in finding the solutions in closed-form of the following system of equations:

possibly containing some trigonometric terms, where β is the vector representing the physical parameters of the robot, q is the vector of the joint generalized coordinates, and ξ = [x y z] is the vector of the end-effector coordinates. The function h can directly be determined by inspecting the matrix Q0,3 (in particular, the entries corresponding to d0,3, considered as functions of the physical parameters β of the robot arm and of the joint generalized coordinates q). Solving the inverse kinematics means finding all joints generalized coordinates q such that the end-effector is in the desired location in the workspace, where the workspace is the set of all positions that can be reached.

The techniques outlined in Chapter 1 can directly be used to perform such a task. In fact, assume, without loss of generality, that the joint generalized coordinates are ordered so that q1, . . . , qn correspond to rotational joints and qn+1, . . . , qn correspond to linear joints, n̄ ∈ 0, 0 n̄ n. In view of (3.1), if the convention of Denavit–Hartenberg is used in the collocation of the reference frames, one has that h is a three-dimensional vector function whose entries are polynomial functions in the variables qn̄+1, . . . , qn and trigonometric functions in the variables q1, . . . , qn̄.

Although the functions cos(·) and sin(·) are not polynomials, the map

constitute a parameterization of the variety V(c2 + s2 − 1) in 2. Therefore, by repeated applications of the formulas

and applying, for i = 1, . . . , n̄, the substitutions

the forward kinematics (3.2) can equivalently be rewritten as

with p1, p2, p3 ∈ (β, x, y, z)[c1, s1, . . . , cn̄, sn̄, qn̄+1, . . . , qn]. Thus, considering the following ideal in (β, x, y, z)[c1, s1, . . . , cn̄, sn̄, qn̄+1, . . . , qn]:

the methods outlined in Chapter 1 can be used to determine the set of all joints configurations q such that the end-effector is in the desired location ξ = [x y z]⊤, for “almost all” ξ in the workspace and “almost all” physical parameters β of the robot arm. In fact, using the procedures outlined in Chapter 1, one can determine a reduced Gröbner basis of the ideal that can be used to find closedform algebraic inverses of the direct kinematics (3.2). In particular, these expressions can be used at all the points within the workspace wherein the denominator of the rational expressions do not vanish and the arguments of the square roots are positive. Since the algebraic set satisfying these properties is open, these inverses can be used for almost all ξ in the workspace and “almost all” physical parameters β of the robot arm, according to Definition 1.1.2.

The following section shows how this technique can be used to determine the inverse kinematics of some well-known arm-and-body structures.

4.1 Observability of real analytic and polynomial time-invariant systems

Consider the real analytic time-invariant system

where x(t) = [x1(t) . . . xn(t)]⊤ ∈ n and y(t) ∈ are the state vector and the single output at time t ∈ , respectively; h and the n entries of f are real analytic on the whole n; x1, . . . , xn are the state variables. In this chapter, time-invariant means that f and h do not depend explicitly on t, but only on x(t). If f ∈ n[x] and h ∈ [x], then system (4.1) is referred to as a polynomial system. Since the entries of f have continuous partial derivatives on the whole affine space n, by the classical Cauchy Theorem (Cauchy, 1842), for any initial state x◦ ∈ n, there exists a unique solution x(t) of (4.1a) satisfying x(t◦) = x◦ for all times t in an open interval having the initial time t◦ in its interior. Since f and h do not depend on time t, without loss of generality, by a shift of the time axis, the initial time t◦ is always taken equal to 0 in the following when the system is time-invariant. For each initial state x◦ ∈ n, there exists a maximal open interval of time x◦ ⊆ having 0 in its interior and containing any open interval of time along which there exists a solution of (4.1a) satisfying x(0) = x◦. For any pair of initial states ∈ n, the interval is a non-empty open interval of time having 0 in its interior. By the classical Cauchy Theorem, the solution x(t) is analytic at t = 0, as well as y(t) = h(x(t)).

The unique maximal solution of the real analytic system (4.1a) at time t ∈ x◦, from the initial state x◦ ∈ n, is denoted x(t) = ϕf (t, x◦) and is uniquely determined by the initial state x◦. The state solution x(t) = ϕf (t, x◦) satisfies

The observability map of order N + 1, ye,N = ON (x), is injective if it is a one-to-one mapping from n to ON (n). If the observability map of order N + 1 is injective, then there is a left inverse x = (ye,N) from ON (n) to n such that x̂ = ◦ ON (x̂), for all x̂ ∈ n. If ON ∈ N+1[x], a necessary condition for ye,N = ON (x) to be injective is that the Jacobian matrix J(x) = has full column-rank over the field (x), although matrix J(x̂) need not have full column-rank over the field for all x̂ ∈ n.

Hence, special attention must be payed to study the injectivity properties of polynomial maps.

Consider a polynomial map ye,N = kN (x) from n to N+1, with N + 1 n. The objective is to verify if such a map is injective, and, in that case, to compute one of the possible expressions of its left inverse (possibly, the simplest one). This analysis must be carried out on some ambient ring b; for the definition of b, it may be necessary to do some computations on a preliminary ambient ring a, as detailed in the following.

First, let a = [x, ye,N] be the ambient ring, consider the ideal = 〈ye,N − kN (x)〉, and compute the elimination ideal = ∩ [ye,N]. There are three possible cases:

(i) If = 〈〉 (i.e., is the zero ideal), then the entries of kN (x) are algebraically independent, from which one fixes b = (y0, . . . , yN)[x1, . . . , xn] as ambient ring (i.e., the set of polynomials in x, with coefficients that are rational functions of ye,N in (y0, . . . , yN)).

(ii) If ≠ 〈〉 (i.e., is not the zero ideal), there are two possibilities:

(a) If = 〈1〉 (i.e., if coincides with the whole [ye,N]), then V() = (both over and ); since kN (n) ⊆ V(), if it were so, one would have kN (n) = , and this case can be excluded because kN (n) is not empty, being k polynomial.

(b) If ≠ 〈1〉 (i.e., if does not coincide with the whole [ye,N]), then the entries of kN (x) are algebraically dependent, and one must fix an ambient field respecting such constraints. In particular, letting [ye,N] be the ideal coerced into [ye,N], consider the quotient ring = [ye,N]/[ye,N]. Now, take as ambient field the set of all rational functions, with numerator and denominator in , = frac(), and take as ambient ring the set b = [x].

In summary, letting b = (y0, . . . , yN) when = 〈〉 and b = when ≠ 〈〉, one has b = b[x]. Having chosen b as ambient field means that the entries of ye,N have been considered as parameters, whose values are “generic” (according to Definition 1.1.2).

4.8 Fault detection and isolation for a DC motor

The problem of fault detection and isolation for a permanent-magnet direct current (DC) motor is considered in this section. The fault detection and isolation method considered in this section is model-based; in particular, it is assumed that:

(i) The dynamic behavior of a DC motor is described, both if the motor is in a nominal condition (i.e., no fault has occurred) and if the motor is in a faulty condition (i.e., a fault has occurred), by the same nonlinear dynamic system, but characterized by different parameters.

(ii) The nonlinear dynamic system depends on a vector β of some parameters. There are a finite number of nominal and faulty conditions, each one identified by a different vector ; if β = ◦ (◦ is the vector of the nominal parameters), the DC motor is in the nominal condition, whereas if β = i, i ∈ 1 (i is the vector of the faulty parameters in the ith faulty condition), the DC motor is in the ith faulty condition.

(iii) For each i ≠ j, one has i ≠ j; in addition, for each fault i, one and only one entry of i differs from the corresponding entry of ◦, from which the maximum number of possible faults is equal to the number of parameters. The values of the entries of ◦ are known, whereas the value of the entry of i being different from the corresponding entry of ◦ is unknown, taking a faulty value.

The following dynamic model of a DC motor is taken from Liu et al. (2000) and Menini et al. (2015a):

where x1(t) is the armature current and x2(t) is the normalized angular velocity at time t ∈ ; L is the armature inductance, u is the input voltage, Ra is the armature resistance, J is the normalized rotor inertia moment, fp is the aerodynamic friction coefficient, fr is the friction coefficient caused by the conditions of the bearing lubrication, T0 is the no-load torque, T2 is the load torque, KT and Ke are coefficients. All throughout this section, it is assumed that such parameters are constant.

Therefore, which failure has occurred can be determined by finding out which output embedding assumes the smallest absolute value when evaluated on . 1. The entry ϕ1(t) is

(a) equal to 0, if |g(◦, )| ϵ, from which one concludes that the motor is in the nominal condition;

(b) equal to i, if |g(◦, )| > ϵ, |gi(◦, )| ϵ and |gj(◦, )| > ϵ, for all j ≠ i, from which one concludes that the motor is in the faulty condition corresponding to a sufficiently high perturbation of the parameter βi;

(c) equal to −1, in all the other cases, from which one concludes that the faulty condition has not been identified.

(b) equal to the estimate x̌2(t) = wi(◦, ) of the state variable x2(t), otherwise.

These DAEs can be solved (either in closed-form or numerically) using the methods given in Kunkel and Mehrmann (2006) and references therein. 5.3 Immersion into LIS form up to a finite order

By Remark 5.2.1, the coefficients of the expressions given in Tables 5.1 and 5.2 provide necessary and sufficient conditions for solvability of Problem 5.1.1 through Algorithm 5.2.2. However, if such conditions do not hold, it may still be possible to compute an immersion that recasts the polynomial system (5.1) into the LIS form (5.2), apart from higher-order terms. Namely, system (5.1) is LIS up to order d ∈ 0, if it can be recast into a system of the form ż(t) = f̃(z)(t), where f̃ : ν → ν is such that its Taylor expansion up to order d, denoted f̃d, is

for some mapping ψi : → , i = 1, . . . , ν. Clearly, if system (5.1) is LIS, then it is LIS up to order d, for any d ∈ 0, whereas the converse need not hold (see, e.g., Example 5.3.1, where a system that is not LIS, but is LIS up to order 3, is given).

Hence, consider the following problem.

6.2 The method of the Lagrange multipliers

The method of the Lagrange multipliers for the computation of the extremum points of a function subject to some equality constraints can be introduced as follows.

Suppose that f(x) and g(x) are differentiable single functions on the whole n, with continuous partial derivatives, let Jf = and Jg = , and denote Jf,i and Jg,i their entries, respectively. Assume that the problem is to find a local maximum f⋆ of f (finding a local minimum of f is equivalent to find a local maximum of −f) subject to the constraint g = 0,

Let x̂⋆ ∈ n be such that f(x̂⋆) = f⋆.

Under the assumption that Jg(x̂⋆) ≠ 0, the method of the Lagrange multipliers consists in introducing a new function (called the Lagrange function and considered as a function of (x, λ)),

which incorporates both the function to be maximized and the constraint, where λ is an additional single variable, called a Lagrange multiplier. Under some conditions, x̂⋆ is a solution to problem (6.2) only if it is an unconstrained critical point of fe (it is noted that fe need not have an unconstrained local maximum, although one is assuming that f subject to the constraint g = 0 has a local maximum).

The reasoning given in the previous page can be justified as follows. Suppose that x = X(ℓ), where ℓ is a single variable, is a parameterization of the constraint around the constrained local maximum, i.e., g(X()) = 0, for all ∈ , where is an open interval in having ⋆ as an interior point, and X(⋆) = x̂⋆. Let F(ℓ) = f(X(ℓ)) and G(ℓ) = g(X(ℓ)). Since G() = 0, for all ∈ , one has Jg(X()) · X′() = 0, for all ∈ , where X′ = . Since, by construction, f⋆ is the unconstrained local maximum of F(ℓ), one has = 0, from which Jf(X(⋆)) · X′(⋆) = 0. Roughly speaking, under the assumption that X′(⋆) ≠ 0, from the above reasoning, one has that the vectors (X(⋆)) and (X(⋆)) are both perpendicular to X′(⋆), and, therefore, are parallel; hence, there exist ∈ , with () ≠ (0, 0), such that

If Jg(x̂⋆) ≠ 0, then one takes = 1 and , for some i such that Jg,i(x̂⋆) ≠ 0, otherwise one takes λf = 0 and λg = 1. If (6.3) holds with = 0, and, therefore = 1, then f⋆ is an unconstrained local maximum of f.

Since Jf points to the direction of steepest increase of f, Jf can be thought of as the “good direction”, whereas Jg can be thought of as the “bad direction”, because following the direction Jg the constraint is violated. If x̂⋆ is a point satisfying the constraint such that f(x̂⋆) is a local maximum of f on the constraint g = 0, then one cannot get any local increase of f starting from f⋆, because the “good direction” and the “bad direction” are the same.

Definition 6.2.1. Given a function g(x), one has:

(6.2.1.1) A point x̂ ∈ n such that Jg(x̂) = 0 is called a critical point of g.

(6.2.1.2) A point x̂ ∈ n such that g(x̂) = 0 and Jg(x̂) = 0 is called a singular point of g.

A polynomial g ∈ [x] has no singular points if and only if V(〈g, Jg〉) = ; in particular, if 〈g, Jg〉 = 〈1〉, then V(〈g, Jg〉) = V(〈1〉) = , and, therefore, g has no singular points.

Definition 6.2.2. A constraint g = 0 is called regular if V(〈g, Jg〉) = .

Clearly, if 〈g, Jg〉 = 〈1〉, then the constraint g = 0 is regular.

Definition 6.3.1. The following set is referred to as a semi-algebraic set:

Finite unions and intersections of semi-algebraic sets are semi-algebraic. In addition, unlike affine varieties, the complement of a semi-algebraic set is semi-algebraic. Finally, the projection of a semi-algebraic set onto a linear space is semi-algebraic; in particular, also the projection of an affine variety (which is also a semi-algebraic set) onto a linear space is semi-algebraic. Actually, in the following, it is shown that any semi-algebraic set can be thought of as the projection of some affine variety.

Letting ℓ be a dummy single-variable and πx be the projection map which sends (ℓ, x) to x, one has

(3) V(p(x) < 0) = πx(V(ℓ2 · p + 1));

(4) V(p(x) 0) = πx(V(p − ℓ2));

(5) V(p(x) 0) = πx(V(p + ℓ2)).

8.2 f-invariant sets for discrete-time systems

Consider the real analytic, discrete-time (DT), time-invariant system described by the following vector difference equation:

where x(t) = [x1(t) · · · xn(t)]⊤ is the state vector at time t ∈ , and the entries of the vector function f : n → n are real analytic in n; time-invariant means that f does not depend on t, but only on x. If f ∈ n[x], then system (8.9) is referred to as a polynomial DT-system. Since f does not depend on time t, without loss of generality, by a shift of the time axis, the initial time t◦ is always taken equal to 0 in the following. The solution x(t) of the DT-system (8.9) from the initial state x(0) = x◦ ∈ n is x(t) = ψf (t, x◦), where ψf (t, x) is the tth iteration of f(x) (i.e., ψf (0, x) = x, ψf (1, x) = f(x), ψf (2, x) = f ◦ f(x), and so on), with t ∈ 0. The are no questions about the existence and uniqueness of solution for real analytic DT-systems, in the sense that the solution x(t) is defined on the whole 0 and is uniquely determined by the initial state x◦ ∈ n. The function ψf : 〈 n → n is the DT-flow associated with f and satisfies (Menini and Tornambe, 2011)

It is clear that ψf (t, x) is, for any t ∈ 0, a real analytic function of x ∈ n. Unlike CT-systems (i.e., systems represented by differential equations), existence and uniqueness of the solution is only ensured for the forward direction of time, since f need not be injective.

The notion of f-invariance for DT-systems is slightly different from the one for CT-systems.

Definition 8.2.1. For DT-systems, a set (possibly, an affine variety ) in n is

(i) f-invariant, if f() = ,

(ii) positively f-invariant, if f() ⊆ .

Chapter 9

Boolean Networks

9.1 The Galois field 2

Let a and b be arbitrary integers; a is congruent to b modulo 2 (denoted a = b mod 2) if the difference a−b is a multiple of 2. Hence, can be partitioned into two congruence classes, 0 and 1, of all integers congruent to 0 and to 1 modulo 2, respectively. It is possible to define the sum and the product of two congruence classes as a + b= a + b and ab= ab, respectively. Hence, the set {0, 1}, with the sum and the product defined above, is a finite field and is denoted /2.

Let 2 := {0, 1} and let φ : /2 → 2 be the mapping defined by φ(a) = a, for a ∈ {0, 1}. One has that 2, with the field structure induced by φ, is a finite field, which is called the Galois field of order 2.

Let x = [x1 . . . xn]⊤ be a vector of single variables taking values in , i.e., x̂i ∈ 2, i = 1, . . . , n; x is called a Boolean vector. A vector map from to is called Boolean and it can be described assigning at each of the 2n points in one of the 2l points in . A Boolean network is a discrete-time system of the form

9.2.1 Reduced linear representation of Boolean networks

Although the representation through linear immersion of Boolean networks given in (9.5) has several advantages (as, e.g., the possibility of computing the solutions in closed form of the Boolean network and the availability of efficient tools to determine cycles), it has a major drawback: the size of the state. As a matter of fact, system (9.5) has 2n states, whence the dimension of system (9.5) grows exponentially with the number of Boolean variables involved in the network. In order to overcome this issue, it is possible to use algebraic geometry to obtain a reduced linear representation of the Boolean network.

Example 9.2.8. Th-lymphocytes (or Th-cells) are a sub-type of white blood cells that play a crucial role in the adaptive immune system. They support the activity of other immune cells by secreting small proteins (called cytokines), which assist and regulate the active immune response. Such cells, when subject to proper stimulation, can differentiate into Th1 or Th2 cells, which enable cell mediated immunity and humoral responses, respectively, by secreting different cytokines.

9.3 Finite-horizon optimal control for Boolean networks

In this section, a method to find a feedback control law that minimizes a finite-horizon cost function for a Boolean network is given exploiting the dynamic programming algorithm given in Bertsekas (1995) and adapted to Boolean networks in Menini et al. (2016a).

Before discussing the actual procedure to solve this class of optimal control problems, an algebraic geometry procedure to compute the solution to an integer programming problem is reviewed.

Chapter 10

Multi-objective Optimization

10.1 Multi-objective optimization in control system design

The aim of this chapter is to show that the joint use of multi-objective optimization and algebraic geometry allows one to find closed-form solutions to some significant feedback control problems, regarding the following linear time-invariant system:

where A ∈ ν×ν, B ∈ ν×η, C ∈ ς×ν, and ξ(t) ∈ ν, u(t) ∈ η, and y(t) ∈ ς are the state, input, and output vectors at time t, respectively. Let system (10.1a) be stabilizable and detectable and let

where Iν is the ν × ν identity matrix, be the transfer matrix of system (10.1a). Note that it has been assumed, in (10.1a), that there is no a direct connection between the input u and the output y. This assumption has been made for simplicity, but it can be removed through minor modifications of the subsequent Problems 10.1.1 and 10.1.2.

10.1.1 Pole placement with compensators having a fixed structure

Let W (s, x) be the transfer matrix of the feedback control system obtained through the interconnection of F(s) and some controller having a fixed structure G(s, x), where x = [x1 . . . xn]⊤ ∈ Ωp is a vector of design parameters and Ωp is a semi-algebraic set. This class of closed-loop systems includes plants that are controlled through static output feedback, standard regulators, and so on. Let d(s, x) be the monic least common multiple of the denominators of the entries of W (s, x), which is a polynomial in s with coefficients being polynomials in x.

Problem 10.1.1. Let Ωp ⊆ n be a given semi-algebraic set and let d(s, x) be a polynomial in s and x with real coefficients, of degree μ in s, d(s, x) = sμ + ci(x)sμ−i, where the coefficients c1(x), . . . , cμ(x) are polynomials in x, not necessarily monic. Let d̂(s) = sμ + ĉisμ−i, ĉ1, . . . , ĉμ ∈ , be a given Hurwitz monic polynomial. Let 1, . . . , μ ∈ be the (possibly, repeated) roots of d̂(s). Find, if any, x◦ ∈ Ωp such that d(s, x◦) is Hurwitz and the following (non-equivalent) statements holds (possibly, in the Pareto sense as formalized in the subsequent Definition 10.3.1):

(10.1.1.a) the real parts of the roots of d(s, x) attain minimum values at x = x◦;

(10.1.1.b) the squared distances between one root of d(s, x) and 1, between another root of d(s, x) and 2, . . . , and between the remaining root of d(s, x) and μ attain minimum values at x = x◦;

(10.1.1.c) the squared distances (ci(x) − ĉi)2, i = 1, . . . , μ, attain minimum values at x = x◦.

Note that no ordering on the roots of d(s, x) is assumed in Statement (10.1.1.b) of Problem 10.1.1.

If one is able to determine a solution to Statement (10.1.1.a) of Problem 10.1.1, feasible design parameters that achieve fast convergence of the system state solution to zero are obtained; if one is able to determine a solution to either Statements (10.1.1.b) or (10.1.1.c) of Problem 10.1.1, the poles of the closed-loop system are placed as close as possible to some target values1, . . . , μ. Although similar, Statements (10.1.1.b) and (10.1.1.c) of Problem 10.1.1 need not have the same solutions (Menini et al., 2018b). If μ > n, there need not be x◦ ∈ Ωp that satisfies either Statements (10.1.1.a), (10.1.1.b) or (10.1.1.c) of Problem 10.1.1, and, hence, solutions to Problem 10.1.1 have to be understood in the Pareto sense, as in the subsequent Definition 10.3.1 (given in Section 10.3).

10.1.2 Linear quadratic optimization

Let Ci be the ith row of C, yi = Ci ξ, and

Problem 10.1.2 (see Makila, 1989; Dorato et al., 1998). Let at least one of the couples (A, Ci), i = 1, . . . , ς, be detectable. Find, if any, a state feedback u(t) = X◦ ξ(t), X◦ ∈ η×ν, such that the closed-loop system is asymptotically stable and the objectives Ji, i = 1, . . . , ς, attain minimum values.

Since there need not be a gain matrix X◦ that simultaneously minimizes all the cost functions Ji, i = 1, . . . , ς, solutions to Problem 10.1.2 have to be understood in the Pareto sense, as in the subsequent Definition 10.3.1.

Note that, even if just quadratic costs are considered in Problem 10.1.2, several control tasks can be reformulated in such a framework (see Scherer et al., 1997, Section 3 for further details).

10.2 Scalar optimization via algebraic geometry techniques

In this section, several preliminary results that are used in the subsequent Section 10.3 are given.

10.2.1 Path-connected semi-algebraic sets

A set ⊆ n is path-connected if, for any x̂, ŷ ∈ , there is a continuous f : [0, 1] → such that f(0) = x̂ and f(1) = ŷ.

Consider the following two lemmas.

Lemma 10.2.1. Any non-empty semi-algebraic set of n can be decomposed as the union of a finite number of path-connected semi-algebraic sets of n.

Proof. By Bochnak et al. (2013, Proposition 2.4.13) a semi-algebraic set of n is connected if and only if it is path-connected. The lemma follows from Bochnak et al. (2013, Theorem 2.4.5).

Lemma 10.2.2. Let p ∈ m[x]. If a semi-algebraic set Ωp of n is path-connected, then its image through p(·), Ωv = p(Ωp) ⊆ m, is path-connected.

Proof. Let za and zb be in Ωv. Each has at least one pre-image in Ωp, xa and xb such that p(xa) = za and p(xb) = zb, respectively, and by the path connectedness of Ωp, there is a path in Ωp from xa and xb. Applying p to this path yields a path in Ωv from za and zb.

By Lemma 10.2.2, given p ∈ [x], if the semi-algebraic set Ωp is path-connected, then p(Ωp) is an interval of .

10.3 Multi-objective minimization

Consider the multi-objective minimization problem (MOMP)

where f ∈ m[x] is a vector of polynomial objectives,

x in n, and the feasible set Ωp is the set given in (10.4). The entries of f are the criteria that measure the performances of the system and are possibly conflicting. The image through f of the set Ωp is called the attainable set and is defined as

When dealing with the MOMP (10.12), there need not be x◦ ∈ Ωp such that all criteria fi(x), i = 1, . . . , m, are simultaneously minimized at x = x◦. To overcome this issue, the notion of the Pareto optimality has been introduced to deal with multi-criteria optimization (see, e.g., Collette and Siarry, 2013).

Definition 10.3.1. A point x◦ ∈ Ωp is Pareto optimal for the MOMP (10.12) if there is no x̂ ∈ Ωp such that fi(x̂) fi(x◦) for all i = 1, . . . , m, and

for some j ∈ {1, . . . , m}.

Roughly speaking, a point x◦ is Pareto optimal for the MOMP (10.12) if there is no x̂ ∈ Ωp that achieves an improved performance according to a criterion without degrading the performances of at least another criterion. Therefore, according to Definition 10.3.1, solving the MOMP (10.12) is equivalent to determine the set of all its Pareto optimal points. In the following, the set of all Pareto optimal points x◦ is denoted ⊆ Ωp, whereas the image through f of (i.e., the set of the Pareto optimal values) is denoted ⊆ Ωv, = f(); for any f◦ ∈ , there is x◦ ∈ such that f(x◦) = f◦.

Three methods for the solution of the MOMP (10.12) are given. These methods rely on algebraic geometry and allow one to geometrically determine an expression of the Zariski closure of . The method in Section 10.3.1 is an algebraic variant of the weighted-sum-of-objective-functions method (see, e.g., Collette and Siarry, 2013, Section 2.1); the technique given in Section 10.3.2 has some similarities with the hybrid method given in Collette and Siarry (2013, Section 2.5.2); the procedure given in Section 10.3.3 allows one to determine the envelope of a family of hyper–surfaces that contains the set . Unlike the techniques mentioned above, which are essentially based on numerical procedures, the methods given in this chapter provide exact, closed-form solutions to the MOMP (10.12). Finally, an algorithm, which uses the Contact Theorem 10.3.1 to determine the points of this affine variety that are in and the corresponding vectors in , is given in Section 10.3.4.

10.4 Solving control MOMPs

To find a solution to Statements (10.1.1.a) and (10.1.1.b) of Problem 10.1.1, one needs a symbolic expression that relates the roots in s of d(s, x) and x. By the Abel–Ruffini Theorem, if the degree μ of d(s, x) in s is greater than 4, then there need not be a formula involving only radicals that relates the roots of d with the parameters x. The method presented in Section 10.4.1 is a variant of a method used in algebraic geometry for dealing with symmetric polynomials, so to obtain implicit, but symbolic, expressions of the roots of a polynomial, being already in the Gröbner basis form.

Chapter 11

Distance to Internal Instability of Linear Time-Invariant Systems Under Structured Perturbations

11.1 Introduction

The objective of this chapter is the study of the distance of linear time-invariant systems to internal instability (Menini et al., 2020a). This study has a very long history in the literature (see, e.g., Loan, 1985; Gryazina et al., 2008). A continuous-time linear time-invariant system

is exponentially stable if and only if all eigenvalues of its dynamic matrix A have negative real part. In many cases of theoretical and practical interest, only the nominal value A◦ ∈ n×n of A is known, and the difference δA = A−A◦ represents unstructured perturbations from the nominal situation.

On the other hand, in several other cases (e.g., when dealing with mechanical and electrical systems in which the matrix entries are functions of some physical quantities), it is of interest to allow for structured perturbations of the nominal system, i.e., to let the entries of the matrix A vary in a structured way depending on a few uncertain parameters. In both cases, under the assumption that the nominal system is exponentially stable, it is important to know how large the perturbations may be still preserving the exponential stability of the perturbed system.

The aim of this chapter is to extend the analysis already available in the unstructured case (that is briefly reviewed in Section 11.2) to the structured one, allowing the parameters to affect the system in a polynomial way. The main aspects of the chapter can be summarized as follows:

(i) Both continuous-time and discrete-time linear time-invariant systems are considered.

(ii) The uncertain parameters affect the system equations in a polynomial way,

where Δ is either the time derivative (in the continuous-time case) or the one-step forward shift operator (in the discretetime case), and the entries of E(β), A(β) are polynomial functions of a vector β of parameters.

(iii) If the system is well connected (Doyle et al., 2013) (i.e., det(E(β)) ≠ 0), then

thus including the case of the unknown parameters affecting the system in a rational way.

(iv) The unstructured case can be included in the analysis as a sub-case letting the entries of E − E◦ and A − A◦ (where ◦ denotes the nominal case) be the uncertain parameters.

(v) General distance functions in the parameter space can be adopted, including the Euclidean distance.

(vi) The internal exponential stability (i.e., well-posedness and exponential stability) is considered.

(vii) The problem of computing the distance of a nominal system to internal instability is reformulated as the problem of computing the distance of a point to an affine variety.

(viii) A method is given to compute the distance of the nominal system to internal instability.

(ix) Two methods are given for choosing the nominal system in the center (both analytic and Chebyshev centers are considered) of one of the possible compact connected components of the domain of stability, so that the nominal system is sufficiently far from instability. Note that choosing the system model as E(β) Δx(t) = A(β) x(t) allows one to tackle both differential-algebraic systems and the cases when the loss of well-posedness is due to the interconnection of internal sub-systems (Doyle et al., 2013).

Therefore, the techniques proposed in this chapter can be used to study the distance to internal instability of differential-algebraic, linear, time-invariant systems whose dynamic matrices depend on some parameters, either in a polynomial or rational way.

Several other types of metrics have been used in the literature to measure the distance between two systems, such as the gap (Georgiou and Smith, 1990), the graph (Vidyasagar, 1984), and the ν-gap metrics (Vinnicombe, 1993). Unlike these metrics, which account for the distance between the transfer functions of the nominal and the perturbed systems, the squared distance functions considered here (see Definition 11.4.1) account for the distance between the nominal and the perturbed values of the system parameters, so that the measure of robustness is based on quantities that have a direct physical meaning (possibly suitably weighted).

11.2 Related work in the unstructured case

Allowing complex unstructured perturbations δA ∈ n×n, the complex unstructured distance to instability is measured through the complex radius of stability, which is given by (Loan, 1985)

The above formula is particularly useful because it can be extended to cover the class of structured perturbations given by δA = B◦ K C◦, where the real nominal matrices C◦, A◦, B◦ have compatible dimensions and K is a real matrix with uncertain entries. In particular, if

if a static output feedback u(t) = K y(t) is considered, the closed-loop system is given by

Hence, although the parameters linearly affect the perturbation δA = B◦ K C◦, the important case of closed-loop systems under uncertain static output feedback is covered by the uncertainty δA = B◦ K C◦. Clearly, the linearity of the perturbation yielded the above nice results.

With any perturbation δA, one can associate the number N(δA) of eigenvalues of A = A◦ + δA having negative real part; clearly, N(δA) ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n}, and the exponential stability of the system corresponds to N(δA) = n: the domain of stability is the set of all perturbations δA for which N(δA) = n. The number N(δA) can only change in correspondence of the perturbations for which the roots of the characteristic polynomial of A have zero real part. The set of all these points is called the boundary of the D-decomposition of the uncertain parameter space. The boundary of the domain of stability is a subset of the boundary of the D-decomposition (Gryazina and Polyak, 2006; Gryazina et al., 2008).

11.7 Choosing the nominal point

In the previous sections, the nominal value ◦ of the parameters has been assumed to be given; on the other hand, in this section, ◦ is computed by finding a specialization in Ω that is one of the “farthest” (in some sense to be specified) from the boundary ∂Ω of Ω. Consider the set

Since is semi-algebraic, it can uniquely be decomposed (see Grigor’Ev and Vorobjov Jr, 1988) as the disjoint union of its components of connectivity,

where i ∩ j = if i ≠ j, and i is connected, i, j ∈ {1, . . . , σ}. Polynomial hp has constant sign in each i, and the domain of stability Ω is the union of some of these components of connectivity. Let ◦ ∈ i, then i is a connected component of Ω if and only if p(s, ◦) is well-posed and Hurwitz. Clearly, one can define a local center for each connected component i of Ω that is “farthest” from ∂i, and then a global center choosing a local center that is “farthest” from ∂Ω.

Following Luenberger et al. (1984) and Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004), two alternatives for “farthest” are considered: the analytic centers and the Chebyshev centers.

The following theorem provides some mild conditions guaranteeing that the analytic centers are in the interior of .

Theorem 11.7.2. Let i be one of the connected component of ; if i is non-empty and i ∪ ∂i is compact, then there is an analytic center c in i.

Proof. Without loss of generality, let hp() > 0 for all ∈ i. Since i is non-empty and i ∪ ∂i is compact, the continuous function hp(β) takes a maximum value on i ∪ ∂i; such a maximum value must necessarily be positive. This implies that the maximum value of hp is not attained on the boundary ∂i, since hp() = 0 along ∂i, and, hence, it is attained on an interior point of i.

Once the set of the candidate analytic centers c has been computed, to find the farthest analytic centers it is sufficient to evaluate hp(c), so to choose the candidates that minimize the potential function U(·).

Hilbert posed a generalization of his results as the 17th Problem: “must any PSD form p be an SOS of rational functions?” A positive answer was given in Artin (1927) in a rather abstract way. Pólya (1928) gave an explicit solution to the Hilbert 17th Problem for “even” PD forms, using a result that is now known as the Pólya Theorem (Hardy et al., 1952). Later, the Pólya Theorem was used to directly prove that a (not necessarily even) PD form is an SOS of rational functions (Habicht, 1939). Note that, when dealing with polynomials, there is no loss of generality in considering, as in this chapter, only forms, because the properties of being PSD and SOS are transferred upon de-homogenization and preserved upon homogenization. Nevertheless, the property of being PD is not preserved upon homogenization. Due to the above cases, one might guess that “most” PSD forms are SOS, but Blekherman (2006) showed that, for sufficiently high values of d, there exist more PSD forms than SOS’s and that the “difference” between grows as the number of variables increases.

The Gram matrix method (Choi et al., 1995), which originated from the term-inspection method (Reznick, 1978), is one of the fundamental steps that allows the automatic construction of SOS’s. The Gram matrix method consists in the observation that if a form p of total degree 2d can be represented as an SOS,

with the hi’s being forms of total degree d, one can associate with such an SOS a matrix Q, called the Gram matrix, which depends on the coefficients of the forms hi. As a matter of fact, let be the vector having as entries the (arbitrarily) ordered monomials in x of total degree d, so that

let B be the matrix having as ith row and h the vector having hi as ith entry,

The Gram matrix associated with is

by construction, B⊤B is always positive semi-definite (PSD), and uniquely determined, once the order of the monomials and of the forms hi are fixed. Hence, by considering all possible expressions of p as SOS and the corresponding Gram matrices, one obtains a set of Gram matrices associated with p. If p is an SOS, then m is the minimum integer such that for some forms hi’s, if and only if m is the minimum rank of Q, as Q varies in such an m is called the length of p. The Gram matrix method has firstly been implemented in Powers and Wörmann (1998), according to the following observation. Let be the set of all symmetric matrices P such that

clearly, and, in particular, any PSD matrix P ∈ is a Gram matrix of p. Given , there is a finite number κ + 1 of symmetric matrices P0, P1, . . . , Pκ such that
