Semi-algebraic sets can precisely be characterized by means of quantifier elimination and cylindrical algebraic decomposition (Collins, 1975), which, however, present an inherent high complexity. Another fundamental step for obtaining an efficient procedure for the computation of an SOS is realizing that is convex (Nesterov, 2000; Parrilo, 2000) and that there is a strong relationship between convex optimization problems (semi-definite Programs) and SOS decompositions; it is worth pointing out that SPD methods also make it possible to optimize over SOS polynomials. Since convex optimization problems can efficiently be solved by interior point methods (Vandenberghe and Boyd, 1996), the computation of an SOS decomposition of a form is now tractable. There exist several efficient solvers (e.g., SeDuMi, see Sturm, 1999) of convex optimization problems and two MATLAB toolboxes that are widely used for their modeling and solution, SOSTOOLS (Papachristodoulou et al., 2013) and YALMIP (Löfberg, 2009), by interfacing with external solvers. Thanks to such toolboxes, various techniques based on SOS decompositions are nowadays used in many applications of systems and control theory (Prajna et al., 2004; Raman et al., 2016).

Typically, the output of the algorithms described above is numerically approximated, and this may be a problem in some cases. One possibility to obtain an exact weighted SOS (wSOS) with positive weights (wSOS+) decomposition, over the field of rational numbers, is proposed in Peyrl and Parrilo (2008, 2007) (see, also, Kaltofen et al., 2012; Powers, 2011), where, under a strict feasibility assumption, it is shown that an approximate solution of the semi-definite program is sufficient to obtain a rational wSOS+ decomposition of the given polynomial. Qualitatively, the strict feasibility assumption consists in assuming that there are interior points of sufficiently far from the boundary of . Recently, it has been shown (see Henrion et al., 2016) that LMI feasibility problems can be solved without a strict feasibility assumption. If p can be rewritten as a wSOS with m∗ squares, but not less, then m∗ is called the w-length of p (Menini et al., 2018a).

The idea pursued in this chapter is to construct wSOS+ decompositions without passing through numerically approximated computations, working in some field containing the rationals and contained in the reals. When moving from to such a , the complexity of the problem increases, e.g., one important question is: “if p is a polynomial with coefficients in that is SOS over (possibly, = ), then is p also a sum of squares over ?” If is a totally real field, Galois over , Hillar (2009) showed that the answer is positive, whereas the answer is negative if = , as shown in Scheiderer (2012), where it is proved that the form

is a sum of two squares over the reals (actually, over a totally real field, not Galois over ), but it is not a sum of any number of squares over the rationals; this is just one of the difficulties that arise when moving from to . A complete answer to the above question has been given in the case of forms with n = 2 (i.e., upon de-homogenization, for univariate polynomials with rational coefficients); Landau (1906) showed that any PSD form of two variables, with rational coefficients, can always be written as a sum of 8 squares over the rationals, and such a result was improved by Pourchet (1971), who demonstrated that 5 squares are sufficient. Some algorithms for the computation of SOS decompositions of bivariate forms over the rationals can be found in Menini and Tornambe (2015).

12.6 Randomly generated experiments

Randomly generated experiments have been carried out to compare either Algorithm 12.4.1 in the case n > m or the procedure presented in Section 12.3 in the case n m, both implemented in Macaulay2 (Grayson and Stillman, 2020), with the MATLAB toolboxes SOSTOOLS (Papachristodoulou et al., 2013) and YALMIP (Löfberg, 2009), interfaced with the solver SeDuMi (Sturm, 1999). All experiments have been carried out on a laptop running Windows 8.1, with an Intel Core i5 3210M CPU (2.50 GHz) processor and 6 GB of RAM DDR3. In each experiment, the weights wi and the coefficients of the forms hi ∈ [x]d, i = 1, . . . , m, have been generated as random integers uniformly distributed in the intervals [1, 100] and [−100, 100], respectively, and the corresponding form p ∈ [x]=2d has been obtained by substituting such values in For 2d = 4, n varies in {2, . . . , 6} and m varies in {1, . . . , 4}, for a total of 20 tests, whose results are reported in Table 12.2; for 2d = 6, n varies in {2, . . . , 5} and m varies in {1, 2, 3}, for a total of 12 tests, whose results are reported in Table 12.3; for 2d = 8, n varies in {2, 3, 4} and m varies in {1, 2, 3}, for a total of 9 tests, whose results are reported in Table 12.4. In each test, the same set of 1000 forms (100 forms only for the more complex test 2d = 8, n = 4, m = 3), randomly generated as above, has been used as input to

Each table corresponds to the same value of 2d, and the entries of the subtables (a), (b), (c) and (d) (corresponding to the same pair m, n) are referred to the same test. Each entry of the sub-tables reports two numbers: the average execution time (either with a wSOS+ decomposition or with a failure) and the % of exact rational wSOS+ decompositions obtained when Alg. Geom. or SOSTOOLS rational are used, and the percentage of approximated wSOS+ decompositions obtained without running into numerical errors, when SOSTOOLS numeric or YALMIP numeric are used.

Table 12.4: Results of the randomly generated experiments: Case 2d = 8.

The procedures proposed in this chapter (case (a) in the tables) give an exact certificate of the forms being PSD in 100% of the cases, with different execution times depending on the complexity of the analyzed form. If 2d = 4, Algorithm 12.4.1 produces an exact rational wSOS+ with ranging from 0.16ms (when n = 2, m = 1) to 15.33s (when n = 6, m = 4), whereas the procedure presented in Section 12.3 produces an exact certificate of being PSD with ranging from 2, 61ms (when n = 2, m = 2) to 47.16s (when n = 4, m = 4). Similar results are obtained for 2d = 6 and 2d = 8, with the worst average execution time obtained with Algorithm 12.4.1 when 2d = 8, n = 4, m = 3, with = 2.04hours. In this case, the considered 100 forms p are constituted each by 165 monomials of total degree 8, and the three forms h1, h2, h3 have 35 monomials, with a total of 108 coefficients (including the weights) to be determined. For the test 2d = 8, n = 4, m = 3, SOSTOOLS rational gives an exact rational wSOS+ in 6% of the cases, SOSTOOLS numeric gives an approximate wSOS+, without running into numerical errors, in 8% of the cases, and YALMIP numeric gives an approximate wSOS+, without running into numerical errors, in 4% of the cases. SOSTOOLS rational, SOSTOOLS numeric and YALMIP numeric work very well when n m: they give exact rational wSOS+’s, and approximate wSOS+’s without running into numerical errors, in 100% of the cases, with a maximum average execution time of 0.83s; in addition, such average execution times are often lower than the corresponding times when the procedure presented in Section 12.3 is used. Contrarily, SOSTOOLS rational, SOSTOOLS numeric and YALMIP numeric do not work well when n > m, and in particular in many cases no exact rational wSOS+, and no approximate wSOS+ without running into numerical errors, is obtained. From these results, it can be concluded that Algorithm 12.4.1 is complementary to the two MATLAB toolboxes SOSTOOLS and YALMIP, with the solver SeDuMi.

12.8 wSOS+ decomposition through tools of linear algebra

The main objective of this section is to provide a technique based on linear algebra to find, if any, a wSOS+ decomposition of a given form of total degree 2d whose length m is lower than the number n of variables (Menini et al., 2019d). To reach such a result, in Section 12.8.1 a procedure is given to compute the Gröbner basis up to total degree d of the saturation of the gradient ideal by a variable through the reduced row echelon form. Similar results are used in Section 12.8.2 to determine a polynomial representation of a form of total degree 2d in terms of forms of total degree d. In Section 12.8.3, a linear algebra tool to perform the “completing the square” procedure is proposed. Finally, in Section 12.8.4 these three techniques are combined to outline a procedure able to find, if any, a wSOS+ decomposition of a “generic” form of total degree 2d in the case n > m. Examples are reported to illustrate the proposed methods.

12.8.1 Saturation

The following Algorithm 12.8.1 summarizes the technique given in Fact 12.8.1 to perform Step 1 of Algorithm 12.4.1 through linear algebra (entailing also its possible failure).

It is worth noting that if N (to be fixed at Step 1) is not known a priori, the procedure presented in Algorithm 12.8.1 has to be repeated for N = 1, 2, 3, . . . until the output of the algorithm obtained taking N = N⋆ equals the one gathered with N = N⋆ + 1, for some N⋆ ∈ 0.

Remark 12.8.1. If fixed precision numbers are used, the computations carried out by Algorithm 12.8.1 may be inaccurate. As a matter of fact, the matrix Λ defined at Step 5 of Algorithm 12.8.1 may be very ill-conditioned (essentially due to the fact that, in its rational reduced row echelon form, ratios of large integer numbers appear), thus possibly leading to inaccurate results for the computation of the polynomials g1, . . . , gm. 12.8.3 Linear algebra implementation of the “completing the square” procedure

In this section, a linear algebra technique, which provides the same results of the “completing the square” procedure to be executed at Step 9 of Algorithm 12.4.1, is given. Unlike the procedure given in Rajwade (1993, Theorem 6.1), such a technique is guaranteed to provide a wSOS decomposition of the input form only if it can be represented as a wSOS+, whereas it may fail if the input form p is not sign definite. Such a limitation of the proposed method is not an issue in practical applications, where the attention is focused just on wSOS+ (see, for instance, Prajna et al., 2004, 2007; Papachristodoulou and Prajna, 2002, 2005; Chesi, 2010; Ahmadi et al., 2014; Raman et al., 2016).

Consider the following technical lemma.

Lemma 12.8.1. Let p(x) = z⊤(x)Az(x), where z(x) = Jx, J ∈ m×n, and A ∈ m×m. Without loss of generality, assume that n m, that J is in the reduced row echelon form, that it has full rowrank, and that A is symmetric and invertible. Hence, is the reduced row echelon form of from which the zero rows have been removed.

Proof. Since p is quadratic, one has

i.e., J is the reduced row echelon form of H, where the zero rows are removed.

Let H be the Hessian matrix of the quadratic form p and let J = r(H) be its row reduced echelon form from which the zero rows have been removed. Using the relation given in (12.8), one has that the matrix

is such that p(x) = x⊤J⊤AJx. Note that, given a quadratic form p, the matrix A is unique, due to the uniqueness of the reduced row echelon form J, and is non-singular. Since such a matrix need not be diagonal (and, hence, the obtained expression need not be a wSOS), consider the following lemma that proposes a factorization of the matrix A as the product of triangular matrices times a diagonal one.

Lemma 12.8.2 (Cholesky Factorization, Meyer, 2000). Let A ∈ m×m be a positive definite, symmetric matrix. Thus, A can uniquely be decomposed into a product of the following form (called LDLT decomposition of A):

where L ∈ m×m is lower triangular, with Li,i = 1, i = 1, . . . , m, and D ∈ m×m is diagonal.

Note that an LDLT decomposition of non-definite matrices can successfully be computed even if the matrix A depends on some symbolic parameters. Combining the results given in Lemmas 12.8.1 and 12.8.2, the following Algorithm 12.8.3 allows one to find, if any, a wSOS+ decomposition of a given quadratic form.

Algorithm 12.8.3: The “completing the square” procedure through linear algebra.

Note that also Step 4 of Algorithm 12.8.3 can easily be carried out through linear algebra techniques. As a matter of fact, to determine if A is positive definite, it is sufficient to compute all of its leading minors. If all such determinants are positive, then A is positive definite, otherwise it is not (Possieri and Sassano, 2015).

Remark 12.8.2. It is worth noting that, in principle, a wSOS decomposition of the quadratic form p can directly be obtained computing an LDLT decomposition of the Hessian matrix H. However, since numerical algorithms to compute LDLT decomposition perform better if the input matrix is non-singular, it has been preferred, in Algorithm 12.8.3, to compute the LDLT decomposition of the matrix A (that, by Lemma 12.8.1, is non-singular) rather than the one of H directly.

12.8.4 wSOS+ representation

In this section, the procedures given in Sections 12.8.1, 12.8.2, and 12.8.3 are combined to provide a procedure able to “generically” find a wSOS+ decomposition of a form that can be represented as the weighted sum of m < n squares with positive weights.

By Theorem 12.4.3, if the form p can be represented as p = for some forms h1, . . . , hm of total degree d and for some w1, . . . , wm ∈ , with m > n, then Algorithm 12.4.1 “generically” returns a wSOS representation of p. By Fact 12.8.1, Algorithm 12.8.1 allows one to carry out Step 1 of Algorithm 12.4.1 of such a procedure, by Fact 12.8.2, Algorithm 12.8.2 allows one to execute Step 7 of Algorithm 12.4.1 and, by Lemmas 12.8.1 and 12.8.2, Algorithm 12.8.3 allows one to perform the “completing the square” procedure. Therefore, the following Algorithm 12.8.4 (which combines Algorithms 12.8.1, 12.8.2, and 12.8.3) allows one to find, if any, a wSOS+ decomposition of a given form.

Algorithm 12.8.4: wSOS+ decomposition through linear algebra.
